## <span class="num">17.2.1</span> Field Extensions

:::definition{17.2.1} Field extension and degree
A ***field extension*** $L/K$ is a field $L$ containing a field $K$ as a subfield (Chapter 4). Then $L$ is a vector space over $K$, and the ***degree*** of the extension is $[L:K] = \dim_K L$. The extension is ***finite*** if $[L:K] < \infty$.
:::

:::proposition{17.2.2} Tower law
If $K \subseteq L \subseteq M$ are fields and $[M:L]$ and $[L:K]$ are finite, then $[M:K] = [M:L] \cdot [L:K]$.
:::

:::proof
Let $e_1, \ldots, e_m$ be a basis of $M$ over $L$ and $f_1, \ldots, f_n$ a basis of $L$ over $K$. We show that the products $f_j e_i$ form a basis of $M$ over $K$. Every $x \in M$ is $x = \sum_i a_i e_i$ with $a_i \in L$, and each $a_i = \sum_j b_{ij} f_j$ with $b_{ij} \in K$; so $x = \sum_{i,j} b_{ij} f_j e_i$. If $\sum_{i,j} b_{ij} f_j e_i = 0$ with $b_{ij} \in K$, then $\sum_i \bigl(\sum_j b_{ij} f_j\bigr) e_i = 0$, so each $\sum_j b_{ij} f_j = 0$ by independence of the $e_i$ over $L$, and then each $b_{ij} = 0$ by independence of the $f_j$ over $K$.
:::

:::definition{17.2.3} Algebraic and transcendental elements
Let $L/K$ be a field extension and $\alpha \in L$. Then $\alpha$ is ***algebraic*** over $K$ if $f(\alpha) = 0$ for some nonzero $f \in K[x]$, and ***transcendental*** over $K$ otherwise.
:::

For $\alpha \in L$, evaluation $\ev_\alpha : K[x] \to L$, $f \mapsto f(\alpha)$, is a ring homomorphism, and $\alpha$ is algebraic exactly when its kernel is nonzero. For $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in L$, we write $K(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n)$ for the smallest subfield of $L$ containing $K$ and $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ (the intersection of all such subfields).

:::proposition{17.2.4} Minimal polynomial
Let $\alpha \in L$ be algebraic over $K$. There is a unique monic polynomial $m_\alpha \in K[x]$ with $\ker(\ev_\alpha) = (m_\alpha)$, the ***minimal polynomial*** of $\alpha$ over $K$. It is the monic polynomial of least degree with $m_\alpha(\alpha) = 0$, and it is irreducible.
:::

:::proof
The kernel of $\ev_\alpha$ is a nonzero ideal of $K[x]$, which is a PID (Example [17.1.10](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#example-17-1-10) and Theorem [17.1.12](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#theorem-17-1-12)); a generator is a nonzero element of least degree, and exactly one generator is monic, since two monic polynomials that divide each other are equal. If $m_\alpha = fg$ with $\deg f, \deg g < \deg m_\alpha$, then $f(\alpha)g(\alpha) = 0$ in the field $L$, so $f(\alpha) = 0$ or $g(\alpha) = 0$, contradicting minimality. And $m_\alpha$ is not a unit, since $\deg m_\alpha \geq 1$. So $m_\alpha$ is irreducible.
:::

:::proposition{17.2.5} Simple algebraic extensions
If $\alpha$ is algebraic over $K$ with minimal polynomial $m_\alpha$ of degree $n$, then $$K(\alpha) = \{f(\alpha) : f \in K[x]\} \cong K[x]/(m_\alpha),$$ and $[K(\alpha) : K] = n$, with basis $1, \alpha, \alpha^2, \ldots, \alpha^{n-1}$.
:::

:::proof
By Proposition [17.1.2](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#proposition-17-1-2), the image $K[\alpha] = \{f(\alpha) : f \in K[x]\}$ of $\ev_\alpha$ is isomorphic to $K[x]/(m_\alpha)$. Since $m_\alpha$ is irreducible, $(m_\alpha)$ is maximal (Corollary [17.1.14](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#corollary-17-1-14)), so $K[\alpha]$ is a field. It contains $K$ and $\alpha$, and it is contained in every subfield of $L$ containing them; so $K[\alpha] = K(\alpha)$. Division with remainder by $m_\alpha$ shows that every element of $K(\alpha)$ is $f(\alpha)$ with $f = 0$ or $\deg f < n$, and this $f$ is unique: if $f(\alpha) = g(\alpha)$ with $\deg f, \deg g < n$, then $m_\alpha \mid f - g$, so $f = g$. Hence $1, \alpha, \ldots, \alpha^{n-1}$ is a basis.
:::

:::example{17.2.6} Two simple extensions of $\QQ$
The minimal polynomial of $\sqrt{2}$ over $\QQ$ is $x^2 - 2$, so ${\QQ}(\sqrt{2}) \cong {\QQ}[x]/(x^2 - 2)$ has degree 2 over $\QQ$, with basis $1, \sqrt{2}$. The minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[3]{2}$ over $\QQ$ is $x^3 - 2$, which is irreducible by Eisenstein’s criterion (Proposition [17.1.25](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#proposition-17-1-25)) with $p = 2$; so $[{\QQ}(\sqrt[3]{2}) : \QQ] = 3$.
:::

## <span class="num">17.2.2</span> Splitting Fields and Separability

:::definition{17.2.7} Splitting field
Let $f \in K[x]$ be nonconstant. A ***splitting field*** of $f$ over $K$ is an extension $L/K$ such that $f$ factors into linear factors in $L[x]$ and $L = K(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n)$, where $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are the roots of $f$ in $L$.
:::

:::theorem{17.2.8} Existence and uniqueness of splitting fields
Every nonconstant $f \in K[x]$ has a splitting field over $K$. Any two splitting fields of $f$ over $K$ are isomorphic by an isomorphism that is the identity on $K$.
:::

:::proof Proof of existence
We use induction on $\deg f$. Let $q$ be an irreducible factor of $f$ in $K[x]$, which exists because $K[x]$ is a UFD. By Corollary [17.1.14](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#corollary-17-1-14), $K_1 = K[x]/(q)$ is a field. The composite $K \to K[x] \to K_1$ is a field homomorphism, hence injective (Proposition [4.2.3](/notes/math-55a/4-2-ring-and-field-homomorphisms#proposition-4-2-3)), so we may regard $K_1$ as an extension of $K$; and the class $\alpha$ of $x$ satisfies $q(\alpha) = 0$, hence $f(\alpha) = 0$. In $K_1[x]$ we can write $f = (x - \alpha)f_1$. If $f_1$ is constant, $K_1 = K(\alpha)$ is a splitting field. Otherwise, by induction $f_1$ has a splitting field $L$ over $K_1$. Then $f = (x - \alpha)f_1$ factors into linear factors in $L[x]$, and $L$ is generated over $K$ by $\alpha$ and the roots of $f_1$, because $K_1 = K(\alpha)$; so $L$ is a splitting field of $f$ over $K$.
:::

We omit the proof of uniqueness, which extends an isomorphism of fields one root at a time; see Artin, *Algebra* (2nd edition), Chapters 15 and 16.

:::definition{17.2.9} Normal extension
A finite extension $L/K$ is ***normal*** if every irreducible polynomial in $K[x]$ that has a root in $L$ factors into linear factors in $L[x]$.
:::

:::definition{17.2.10} Separable polynomials and extensions
A nonconstant polynomial $f \in K[x]$ is ***separable*** if it has no repeated roots in a splitting field. An algebraic element $\alpha$ of an extension of $K$ is separable over $K$ if its minimal polynomial is separable, and an extension $L/K$ is ***separable*** if every element of $L$ is algebraic and separable over $K$.
:::

The ***formal derivative*** of $f = \sum_i a_i x^i$ is $f' = \sum_i i a_i x^{i-1}$. The product rule $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$ holds: it is easily checked for monomials and extends by bilinearity.

:::proposition{17.2.11} Separability in characteristic 0
If $\operatorname{char} K = 0$, every irreducible polynomial in $K[x]$ is separable. Hence every algebraic extension of $K$ is separable.
:::

:::proof
If $\alpha$ is a repeated root of $f$ in some extension $L$, then $f = (x - \alpha)^2 g$ in $L[x]$, so $f' = 2(x - \alpha)g + (x - \alpha)^2 g'$ and $f'(\alpha) = 0$. Now let $f \in K[x]$ be irreducible of degree $n \geq 1$, with leading coefficient $a_n$. Since $\operatorname{char} K = 0$, the coefficient $n a_n$ of $x^{n-1}$ in $f'$ is nonzero, so $f' \neq 0$ and $\deg f' < n$. The ideal $(f, f')$ of the PID $K[x]$ is $(d)$ for some $d \mid f$; as $f$ does not divide $f'$, $d$ is not an associate of $f$, so $d$ is a unit because $f$ is irreducible. Thus $1 = af + bf'$ for some $a, b \in K[x]$. If $\alpha$ were a repeated root of $f$, evaluating at $\alpha$ would give $1 = 0$. The second statement follows because minimal polynomials are irreducible (Proposition [17.2.4](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#proposition-17-2-4)).
:::

## <span class="num">17.2.3</span> The Galois Group

For an extension $L/K$, let $\Aut_K(L)$ be the group of field automorphisms $\sigma : L \to L$ with $\sigma|_K = \id_K$.

:::lemma{17.2.12} Automorphisms permute roots
Let $L/K$ be an extension and $f \in K[x]$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. If $\sigma \in \Aut_K(L)$ and $f(\alpha) = 0$, then $f(\sigma(\alpha)) = 0$.
2. If $L = K(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n)$, where $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are the distinct roots of $f$ in $L$, then sending $\sigma$ to the permutation of $\{\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n\}$ that it induces is an injective homomorphism $\Aut_K(L) \to S_n$.
:::

:::proof
(i) Since $\sigma$ is a ring homomorphism fixing the coefficients of $f$, we have $f(\sigma(\alpha)) = \sigma(f(\alpha)) = 0$.

(ii) By (i), $\sigma$ maps the finite set $\{\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n\}$ injectively to itself, hence permutes it, and composition of automorphisms corresponds to composition of permutations. If $\sigma$ fixes every $\alpha_i$, then $\{x \in L : \sigma(x) = x\}$ is a subfield of $L$ containing $K$ and all the $\alpha_i$, so it is $L$, and $\sigma = \id$.
:::

The following theorem characterizes the extensions with as many automorphisms as possible. We state it without proof; see Artin, *Algebra*, Chapter 16.

:::theorem{17.2.13} Galois extensions
Let $L/K$ be a finite extension. Then $|\Aut_K(L)| \leq [L:K]$, and the following are equivalent:

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $|\Aut_K(L)| = [L:K]$;
2. $L/K$ is normal and separable;
3. $L$ is a splitting field over $K$ of a separable polynomial;
4. the elements of $L$ fixed by every element of $\Aut_K(L)$ are exactly the elements of $K$.

Moreover, $L/K$ is normal if and only if $L$ is a splitting field over $K$ of some polynomial.
:::

:::definition{17.2.14} Galois extension and Galois group
A finite extension $L/K$ satisfying the equivalent conditions of Theorem [17.2.13](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#theorem-17-2-13) is ***Galois***, and its ***Galois group*** is $\Gal(L/K) = \Aut_K(L)$. Thus $|\Gal(L/K)| = [L:K]$.
:::

In characteristic 0 the splitting field $L = K(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n)$ of any nonconstant polynomial is a Galois extension of $K$: it is finite by Proposition [17.2.5](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#proposition-17-2-5) and the tower law (each $\alpha_i$ is algebraic over $K(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{i-1})$), normal by the last statement of Theorem [17.2.13](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#theorem-17-2-13), and separable by Proposition [17.2.11](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#proposition-17-2-11).

:::example{17.2.15} Quadratic extensions
Let $d \in \QQ$ be a non-square. Then ${\QQ}(\sqrt{d})$ is the splitting field of $x^2 - d$ over $\QQ$, so it is Galois of degree 2. An automorphism must send $\sqrt{d}$ to a root of $x^2 - d$, that is, to $\pm\sqrt{d}$, so $\Gal({\QQ}(\sqrt{d})/\QQ) = \{\id, \sigma\}$ with $\sigma(\sqrt{d}) = -\sqrt{d}$, and $\Gal({\QQ}(\sqrt{d})/\QQ) \cong \ZZ/2$.
:::

:::example{17.2.16} The splitting field of $x^3 - 2$
Let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$. The roots of $x^3 - 2$ in $\CC$ are $$\alpha_1 = \sqrt[3]{2}, \qquad \alpha_2 = \omega\sqrt[3]{2}, \qquad \alpha_3 = \omega^2\sqrt[3]{2},$$ and they generate $L = {\QQ}(\sqrt[3]{2}, \omega)$, since $\omega = \alpha_2/\alpha_1$; so $L$ is the splitting field of $x^3 - 2$ over $\QQ$, and $L/\QQ$ is Galois. We have $[{\QQ}(\sqrt[3]{2}) : \QQ] = 3$, and $\omega$ is a root of $x^2 + x + 1$ but does not lie in ${\QQ}(\sqrt[3]{2}) \subset \RR$, so $[L : {\QQ}(\sqrt[3]{2})] = 2$ and $[L : \QQ] = 6$ by the tower law. By Lemma [17.2.12](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#lemma-17-2-12), $\Gal(L/\QQ)$ embeds in $S_3$ through its action on $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$; since both groups have order 6, $\Gal(L/\QQ) \cong S_3$.
:::

## <span class="num">17.2.4</span> The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory

:::theorem{17.2.17} Fundamental theorem of Galois theory
Let $L/K$ be a finite Galois extension with Galois group $G = \Gal(L/K)$. There is an inclusion-reversing bijection $$\{\text{intermediate fields } K \subseteq E \subseteq L\} \longleftrightarrow \{\text{subgroups } H \leq G\},$$ given by $E \mapsto \Gal(L/E)$ and $H \mapsto L^H = \{x \in L : \sigma(x) = x \text{ for all } \sigma \in H\}$. If $E$ corresponds to $H$, then:

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $[L:E] = |H|$ and $[E:K] = [G:H]$;
2. $E/K$ is Galois if and only if $H$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, and in that case $\Gal(E/K) \cong G/H$;
3. the intersection of two intermediate fields corresponds to the subgroup generated by the two subgroups, and the smallest field containing both corresponds to the intersection of the subgroups.
:::

:::note
We do not prove the theorem. Besides Theorem [17.2.13](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#theorem-17-2-13), the proof uses the primitive element theorem (every finite separable extension is of the form $K(\alpha)$) and Artin’s lemma ($[L : L^H] = |H|$ for every finite group $H$ of automorphisms of a field $L$).
:::

:::example{17.2.18} Galois correspondence for $x^3 - 2$
Let $L = {\QQ}(\sqrt[3]{2}, \omega)$ as in Example [17.2.16](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#example-17-2-16), and identify $G = \Gal(L/\QQ)$ with $S_3$ through the numbering $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$ of the roots.

- The subgroup $A_3 = \langle (123) \rangle$ has index 2 and is normal. The 3-cycle $\sigma = (123)$ sends $\alpha_1 \mapsto \alpha_2 \mapsto \alpha_3$, so $\sigma(\omega) = \sigma(\alpha_2/\alpha_1) = \alpha_3/\alpha_2 = \omega$; hence $A_3$ fixes ${\QQ}(\omega)$, which has degree $2 = [G : A_3]$, and $A_3$ corresponds to ${\QQ}(\omega)$. Accordingly ${\QQ}(\omega)/\QQ$ is Galois with group $S_3/A_3 \cong \ZZ/2$.
- The subgroup $\langle (23) \rangle$ fixes $\alpha_1$, so it corresponds to ${\QQ}(\alpha_1) = {\QQ}(\sqrt[3]{2})$, which has degree $3 = [G : \langle (23) \rangle]$. Likewise $\langle (13) \rangle$ corresponds to ${\QQ}(\omega\sqrt[3]{2})$ and $\langle (12) \rangle$ to ${\QQ}(\omega^2\sqrt[3]{2})$. These subgroups are not normal, and the three cubic fields are not Galois over $\QQ$; for instance $x^3 - 2$ has the root $\sqrt[3]{2}$ in ${\QQ}(\sqrt[3]{2})$ but does not split there.
:::

## <span class="num">17.2.5</span> Cyclotomic Extensions

Let $n \geq 1$ and $\zeta_n = e^{2\pi i/n}$. The $n$th roots of unity are $\zeta_n^a$ for $a \in \ZZ/n$, and $\zeta_n^a$ is a ***primitive*** $n$th root of unity (one of order exactly $n$) if and only if $a \in (\ZZ/n)^\times$. The $n$th ***cyclotomic polynomial*** is $$\Phi_n(x) = \prod_{a \in (\ZZ/n)^\times} (x - \zeta_n^a),$$ of degree $\varphi(n) = |(\ZZ/n)^\times|$, Euler’s totient. The field ${\QQ}(\zeta_n)$ is the $n$th ***cyclotomic field***. We state the following theorem without proof.

:::theorem{17.2.19} Irreducibility of cyclotomic polynomials
The polynomial $\Phi_n$ has integer coefficients and is irreducible in ${\QQ}[x]$. Hence it is the minimal polynomial of $\zeta_n$ over $\QQ$, and $[{\QQ}(\zeta_n) : \QQ] = \varphi(n)$.
:::

:::proposition{17.2.20} Galois group of a cyclotomic field
The extension ${\QQ}(\zeta_n)/\QQ$ is Galois, and $\Gal({\QQ}(\zeta_n)/\QQ) \cong (\ZZ/n)^\times$: the class of $a$ corresponds to the automorphism $\sigma_a$ with $\sigma_a(\zeta_n) = \zeta_n^a$.
:::

:::proof
The roots of $x^n - 1$ are the powers of $\zeta_n$, so ${\QQ}(\zeta_n)$ is the splitting field of $x^n - 1$ and is Galois over $\QQ$, of degree $\varphi(n)$ by Theorem [17.2.19](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#theorem-17-2-19). An automorphism $\sigma$ sends $\zeta_n$ to a root of its minimal polynomial $\Phi_n$ (Lemma [17.2.12](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#lemma-17-2-12)), so $\sigma(\zeta_n) = \zeta_n^{a}$ for a unique $a \in (\ZZ/n)^\times$, and $\sigma$ is determined by $a$ because $\zeta_n$ generates the field. Since $\sigma_a\sigma_b(\zeta_n) = \sigma_a(\zeta_n^b) = \zeta_n^{ab}$, the map $\sigma \mapsto a$ is an injective homomorphism $\Gal({\QQ}(\zeta_n)/\QQ) \to (\ZZ/n)^\times$. Both groups have order $\varphi(n)$, so it is an isomorphism.
:::

:::note
Since $(\ZZ/n)^\times$ is abelian, every subgroup of it is normal, so by the fundamental theorem every intermediate field of ${\QQ}(\zeta_n)/\QQ$ is Galois over $\QQ$ with abelian Galois group. The Kronecker–Weber theorem, a deep result of algebraic number theory, says conversely that every finite Galois extension of $\QQ$ with abelian Galois group is contained in some cyclotomic field.
:::

## <span class="num">17.2.6</span> Solvability by Radicals

:::definition{17.2.21} Solvable group
A group $G$ is ***solvable*** if it has a chain of subgroups $$G = G_0 \supseteq G_1 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq G_m = \{e\}$$ in which each $G_{i+1}$ is normal in $G_i$ and each quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is abelian.
:::

:::proposition{17.2.22} Subgroups of solvable groups
Every subgroup of a solvable group is solvable.
:::

:::proof
Let $G = G_0 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq G_m = \{e\}$ be as in the definition, and $H \leq G$. The homomorphism $H \cap G_i \to G_i/G_{i+1}$, $x \mapsto xG_{i+1}$, has kernel $H \cap G_{i+1}$, which is therefore normal in $H \cap G_i$, and by the First Isomorphism Theorem (Theorem [3.3.3](/notes/math-55a/3-3-the-isomorphism-theorems#theorem-3-3-3)) the quotient $(H \cap G_i)/(H \cap G_{i+1})$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of the abelian group $G_i/G_{i+1}$. So the chain $H \cap G_i$ shows that $H$ is solvable.
:::

:::example{17.2.23} Symmetric groups
- For $n \leq 4$, $S_n$ is solvable. The groups $S_1$ and $S_2$ are abelian; $S_3 \supseteq A_3 \supseteq \{e\}$ has quotients $\ZZ/2$ and $\ZZ/3$; and $S_4 \supseteq A_4 \supseteq K \supseteq \{e\}$, with $K = \{e, (12)(34), (13)(24), (14)(23)\}$, has quotients of orders 2, 3, 4, namely $\ZZ/2$, $\ZZ/3$, and $K \cong \ZZ/2 \times \ZZ/2$. Each subgroup is normal in the previous one: $A_n$ is the kernel of the sign, and $K$ consists of $e$ and a full conjugacy class of $S_4$.
- $S_5$ is not solvable. If $N$ is a normal subgroup of a group $G'$ with $G'/N$ abelian, then $N$ contains the commutator subgroup $[G', G']$ (Definition [3.3.9](/notes/math-55a/3-3-the-isomorphism-theorems#definition-3-3-9)), since every commutator $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$ maps to the identity of the abelian group $G'/N$. The commutator subgroup $[A_5, A_5]$ is normal in $A_5$ and nontrivial, as $A_5$ is not abelian; since $A_5$ is simple (Theorem [11.4.9](/notes/math-55a/11-4-conjugacy-in-s-n-and-a-n#theorem-11-4-9)), $[A_5, A_5] = A_5$. Now let $S_5 = G_0 \supseteq G_1 \supseteq \cdots$ be a chain as in the definition. Then every $G_i$ contains $A_5$: this holds for $G_0$, and if $G_i \supseteq A_5$, then $G_{i+1} \supseteq [G_i, G_i] \supseteq [A_5, A_5] = A_5$. So the chain never reaches $\{e\}$.
:::

:::definition{17.2.24} Radical extension
An extension $L/K$ is ***radical*** if there is a chain of fields $K = K_0 \subseteq K_1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq K_m = L$ with $K_{i+1} = K_i(\alpha_i)$ and $\alpha_i^{n_i} \in K_i$ for some $n_i \geq 1$. A polynomial $f \in K[x]$ is ***solvable by radicals*** if its splitting field over $K$ is contained in a radical extension of $K$.
:::

So $f$ is solvable by radicals when its roots can be obtained from elements of $K$ by field operations and the extraction of $n$th roots. The following theorem, which we state without proof (see Artin, *Algebra*, Chapter 16), translates this into group theory.

:::theorem{17.2.25} Galois’s criterion
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic 0 and $f \in K[x]$ nonconstant, with splitting field $L$. Then $f$ is solvable by radicals if and only if $\Gal(L/K)$ is a solvable group.
:::

:::lemma{17.2.26} Generating $S_p$
Let $p$ be a prime. A transposition and a $p$-cycle together generate $S_p$.
:::

:::proof
Let $\tau = (a\,b)$ be a transposition and $\sigma$ a $p$-cycle. Since $\sigma$ moves every point through a single cycle, $\sigma^k(a) = b$ for some $1 \leq k < p$. The power $\sigma^k$ has order $p$ (as $p$ is prime), so it is again a $p$-cycle. Renumber the points so that $\sigma^k = (1\,2\,\cdots\,p)$, $a = 1$, and $b = 2$. Conjugating $\tau = (1\,2)$ by the powers of $\sigma^k$ gives $\sigma^{kj}(1\,2)\sigma^{-kj} = (1 + j \;\; 2 + j)$, so the subgroup generated contains all adjacent transpositions $(i \;\; i+1)$, which generate $S_p$ (Proposition [3.4.9](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group#proposition-3-4-9)).
:::

:::example{17.2.27} A quintic with Galois group $S_5$
Let $f = x^5 - 4x + 2 \in {\QQ}[x]$. It is irreducible by Eisenstein’s criterion with $p = 2$. Let $L \subset \CC$ be its splitting field and $G = \Gal(L/\QQ)$. The five roots of $f$ are distinct (Proposition [17.2.11](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#proposition-17-2-11)), and by Lemma [17.2.12](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#lemma-17-2-12) $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $S_5$.

- Since $f(-2) = -22$, $f(0) = 2$, $f(1) = -1$, and $f(2) = 26$, the polynomial $f$ has at least three real roots. Its derivative $5x^4 - 4$ has only two real zeros, so by Rolle’s theorem $f$ has at most three real roots. So $f$ has exactly three real roots and two nonreal, complex conjugate roots.
- Complex conjugation permutes the roots of $f$, which generate $L$, so it maps $L$ to itself and restricts to an element of $G$. It fixes the three real roots and swaps the other two: it is a transposition.
- For a root $\alpha$, $[{\QQ}(\alpha) : \QQ] = 5$ divides $[L : \QQ] = |G|$ by the tower law. So $G$ contains an element of order 5, by Cauchy’s theorem (Corollary [11.5.4](/notes/math-55a/11-5-the-sylow-theorems#corollary-11-5-4)); and the elements of order 5 in $S_5$ are the 5-cycles.

By Lemma [17.2.26](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#lemma-17-2-26), $G \cong S_5$.
:::

:::corollary{17.2.28} The quintic is not solvable by radicals
The polynomial $x^5 - 4x + 2$ is not solvable by radicals over $\QQ$. Consequently there is no formula expressing the roots of a general polynomial of degree 5 in terms of its coefficients using only the field operations and radicals.
:::

:::proof
By Example [17.2.27](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#example-17-2-27), its Galois group is $S_5$, which is not solvable (Example [17.2.23](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#example-17-2-23)); apply Theorem [17.2.25](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#theorem-17-2-25).
:::

:::note
The impossibility of a general formula is the Abel–Ruffini theorem (Abel, 1824); the group-theoretic criterion is due to Galois (1832). For polynomials of degree at most 4, the Galois group is a subgroup of $S_n$ with $n \leq 4$, hence solvable (Proposition [17.2.22](/notes/math-55a/17-2-galois-theory#proposition-17-2-22)), which is why the quadratic formula and the formulas of Cardano and Ferrari exist.
:::

:::exercise{17.2.29} Exercises
<!-- list:paren-decimal -->

1. Compute $\Gal({\QQ}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})/\QQ)$, and draw its lattice of subgroups alongside the lattice of intermediate fields.
2. Show that the Galois group of $x^4 - 2$ over $\QQ$ is isomorphic to the dihedral group $D_4$ of order 8 (Definition [2.2.14](/notes/math-55a/2-2-fundamental-examples#definition-2-2-14)).

:::solution
**(1)** Let $L = {\QQ}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})$. First, $\sqrt{3} \notin {\QQ}(\sqrt{2})$: if $\sqrt{3} = a + b\sqrt{2}$ with $a, b \in \QQ$, then $3 = a^2 + 2b^2 + 2ab\sqrt{2}$, so $ab = 0$; but $b = 0$ would make $\sqrt{3}$ rational, and $a = 0$ would give $b^2 = 3/2$. So $x^2 - 3$ is irreducible over ${\QQ}(\sqrt{2})$, and $[L : \QQ] = 2 \cdot 2 = 4$ by the tower law. The field $L$ is the splitting field of $(x^2 - 2)(x^2 - 3)$, so it is Galois over $\QQ$ and $|\Gal(L/\QQ)| = 4$. An automorphism sends $\sqrt{2} \mapsto \pm\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{3} \mapsto \pm\sqrt{3}$ and is determined by these signs; as there are four automorphisms, all four sign choices occur. Let $\sigma$ change the sign of $\sqrt{2}$ only and $\tau$ that of $\sqrt{3}$ only. Then $\sigma^2 = \tau^2 = \id$ and $\sigma\tau = \tau\sigma$, so $\Gal(L/\QQ) = \{\id, \sigma, \tau, \sigma\tau\} \cong \ZZ/2 \times \ZZ/2$.

The three subgroups of order 2 are $\langle \tau \rangle$, $\langle \sigma \rangle$, $\langle \sigma\tau \rangle$; they fix $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, and $\sqrt{6} = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{3}$ respectively, so they correspond to ${\QQ}(\sqrt{2})$, ${\QQ}(\sqrt{3})$, ${\QQ}(\sqrt{6})$. The two lattices, with corresponding positions matched (the correspondence reverses inclusions):

![fig-17-2-1](/notes/math-55a/figures/fig-17-2-1.svg)

(In the field lattice, larger fields are drawn lower, so that the two pictures correspond position by position.)

**(2)** The polynomial $x^4 - 2$ is irreducible by Eisenstein’s criterion with $p = 2$, and its roots are $\pm\sqrt[4]{2}$ and $\pm i\sqrt[4]{2}$, so its splitting field is $L = {\QQ}(\sqrt[4]{2}, i)$. We have $[{\QQ}(\sqrt[4]{2}) : \QQ] = 4$, and $i \notin {\QQ}(\sqrt[4]{2}) \subset \RR$ is a root of $x^2 + 1$, so $[L : \QQ] = 8$ and $G = \Gal(L/\QQ)$ has order 8. An automorphism sends $\sqrt[4]{2}$ to one of the four roots $i^a\sqrt[4]{2}$ and $i$ to $\pm i$, and is determined by these choices; since there are eight automorphisms, all eight choices occur. Let $\sigma(\sqrt[4]{2}) = i\sqrt[4]{2}$, $\sigma(i) = i$, and let $\tau$ be complex conjugation: $\tau(\sqrt[4]{2}) = \sqrt[4]{2}$, $\tau(i) = -i$. Then $\sigma$ has order 4, $\tau$ has order 2, and $\tau\sigma\tau = \sigma^{-1}$: both sides send $i \mapsto i$ and $\sqrt[4]{2} \mapsto -i\sqrt[4]{2}$. Since $\tau \notin \langle \sigma \rangle$ (it moves $i$), $G = \langle \sigma \rangle \cup \tau\langle \sigma \rangle$, and $\sigma^a\tau^b \mapsto r^a s^b$ is an isomorphism onto $D_4 = \langle r, s \mid r^4 = s^2 = e,\ srs^{-1} = r^{-1} \rangle$. Acting on the four roots, $G$ is a subgroup of $S_4$ of order 8, not all of $S_4$.
:::
:::
